roles.intro: This is a privileged role. Users with this role have access to all administrative features in Microsoft Entra ID, as well as services that use Microsoft Entra identities like the Microsoft Defender portal, the Microsoft Purview portal, Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Skype for Business Online. Global Administrators can view Directory Activity logs. Furthermore, Global Administrators can elevate their access to manage all Azure subscriptions and management groups. This allows Global Administrators to get full access to all Azure resources using the respective Microsoft Entra tenant. The person who signs up for the Microsoft Entra organization becomes a Global Administrator. There can be more than one Global Administrator at your company. Global Administrators can reset the password for any user and all other administrators. A Global Administrator cannot remove their own Global Administrator assignment. This is to prevent a situation where an organization has zero Global Administrators.

Enable a user account (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
Revoke active sessions (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
Force a password reset (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
roles.impact: A role widely handed out for reading and configuring security policy becomes able to disable an account, terminate its live sessions and force a credential reset. Nobody consents to it and no assignment changes; the capability simply arrives. It is the same capability Microsoft carved into the deliberately narrow SOC Identity Responder role in June 2026.
roles.action: Pull the current holders and treat the list as a new privileged role. Move standing assignments into PIM with approval and justification, drop holders who only ever needed to read policy, and alert on Disable account, Revoke sign-in sessions and Reset user password performed by a principal holding Security Administrator.

graph.name: Application.ReadWrite.OwnedBy → authenticationBehaviors.coopEnforcement
graph.before: authenticationBehaviors had no Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy control; COOP enforcement was service-controlled and not app-settable

graph.name: ThreatHunting.Read.All
graph.before: Run hunting queries — advanced hunting only, no access to stored query objects
graph.after: Run hunting queries and read saved hunting queries — plus GET /security/threathunting/queries and GET /security/threathunting/queries/{id}
graph.impact: Saved hunting queries are detection logic. Any application already consented to ThreatHunting.Read.All — typically a SOAR connector or a reporting job — can now enumerate the whole saved-query library without a new consent prompt, which means the team's coverage and its blind spots are readable by anything that could already run a hunt.
graph.action: List every service principal holding ThreatHunting.Read.All and decide, per app, whether reading the saved query library is in scope. Add GET /security/threathunting/queries to the set of Graph calls worth auditing.

Microsoft changed the permission's own consent text in permissions.json at commit f94495e (17 September 2026): “Run hunting queries” becomes “Run hunting queries and read saved hunting queries”, and the scheme gains GET /security/threathunting/queries and GET /security/threathunting/queries/{id}. The permissions reference has not caught up; the change is in Microsoft's permission data, not yet in its documentation.

graph.originNote: Microsoft's own permission data changed. The date is the date of Microsoft's commit to microsoft-graph-devx-content, 17 September 2026, not a date this brief chose.

graph.name: User.ReadBasic.All
graph.consent: Application: admin consent required · Delegated: not required
graph.before: returns a basic set of profile properties and, per Microsoft, also app role assignments and license details — behaviour Microsoft describes as accidental
graph.after: returns the basic profile properties only. App role assignments move to User.Read.All and license details to LicenseAssignment.Read.All
graph.impact: Two effects at once. Applications that quietly relied on the extra data break with no deprecation window — Microsoft states no sunset date. And a low-consent scope (delegated User.ReadBasic.All needs no admin consent) stops exposing licence and app-assignment data, which is reconnaissance material for anyone mapping who holds which application role.
graph.action: List service principals granted User.ReadBasic.All and check which of them read app role assignments or licence data. Applications that legitimately need it must be re-consented to User.Read.All or LicenseAssignment.Read.All, both of which require admin consent — so this is a consent-review task, not a code change.

displayText.Application: Read all users' basic profiles
displayText.Delegated: Read all users' basic profiles

descriptionByType.Application: Allows the app to read a basic set of profile properties of other users in your organization without a signed-in user. Includes display name, first and last name, email address, open extensions, and photo.
descriptionByType.Delegated: Allows the app to read a basic set of profile properties of other users in your organization on behalf of the signed-in user. This includes display name, first and last name, email address and photo.

history.note: Entered the catalog with the permission inventory baseline, parsed from Microsoft’s permissions reference.

Microsoft announced on 1 September 2026 that the permission “accidentally allows the app to read app role assignments and license details of users” and that this access is being removed. The permissions reference already describes only the basic profile properties, so the documentation does not move — the service does.

Microsoft published MC1470871 on 11 September 2026, giving the change its rollout window: general availability worldwide from mid-September 2026, expected complete by late September. The post names the replacement permissions — User.Read.All for app role assignments, LicenseAssignment.Read.All for licence details — and states the reason as a security vulnerability. The catalog entry moves from an announcement with no date to a change already rolling.

graph.dateNote: 1 September 2026 is Microsoft's own publication date for the announcement. No retirement or enforcement date is stated by Microsoft.

displayText.Application: Manage Exchange As Application

descriptionByType.Application: Allows the app to connect to Exchange Online PowerShell without a signed-in user, using app-only authentication.

graph.impact: An app holding this, once paired with an Entra directory role such as Exchange Administrator, runs Exchange Online PowerShell unattended against the whole tenant: transport rules, journaling, mailbox permissions, audit configuration. None of it appears in a Microsoft Graph permission report.
graph.action: Enumerate every service principal with an app role on resource 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000 and confirm each has a business owner. Alert on new appRoleAssignments to that resource, and on Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlets executed by an application identity in the unified audit log.

graph.action: Query appRoleAssignedTo for each of these thirteen appRoleIds across every service principal in the tenant and alert on any grant. graph.name: Group.Read.All → onPremisesExtensionAttributes

descriptionByType.Reach: Microsoft added the onPremisesExtensionAttributes property to the group resource on v1.0. extensionAttribute1 through extensionAttribute15, synchronised from on-premises Active Directory, are now readable on groups.

graph.socNote: No consent prompt fires. Every application already holding Group.Read.All or Group.ReadWrite.All starts seeing on-premises extension attributes on groups it could already read. Those attributes routinely carry cost centre, business unit and classification values, and organisations use them as dynamic membership rule inputs. Re-read what your group-reading applications are entitled to see.

graph.name: AgentIdentityBlueprint.ReadWrite.All → isDisabled

graph.socNote: A kill switch for an agent identity that leaves the object in place. Worth wiring into the agent offboarding runbook now, while the surface is still small: disabling beats deleting when an agent has to be stopped during an investigation and its history has to survive.

roles: Graph API permissions for a role

Microsoft publishes no mapping from a directory role to Graph permissions. The two are separate authorisation planes and do not correspond one to one. Third-party sites compile such a list by hand and say themselves it is not authoritative; this brief does not reproduce a derived list as Microsoft's.
Microsoft publishes no threat narrative per role. Any such text elsewhere is that author's analysis.
The live roleDefinition in your tenant
The action count here is what Microsoft's documentation prints. The role object Graph serves can differ while the docs catch up. Read roleDefinitions in your own tenant before relying on the count.
Whether a PRIVILEGED label was ever removed

Microsoft publishes no change log for the privileged labelling of an individual directory action, and the docs repository's commit history is not reachable from this run. Where this catalog and Microsoft's page disagree on a label, the correction is recorded as this brief's own and no Microsoft-side removal is asserted.
